The central question is whether a KV cache eviction policy — which decides which past token representations to discard when the cache fills — accidentally destroys the structural preconditions that attention sinks depend on. Attention sinks are specific tokens (typically the first one or two positions, often BOS or punctuation) whose keys accumulate disproportionate attention mass not because they are semantically relevant but because they serve as a "drain" that absorbs attention probability that would otherwise be inappropriately high on nearby tokens; this is an architectural necessity that emerges from softmax's inability to produce uniformly low attention. In a sliding window architecture, the window defines which positions are even eligible to receive attention at any step, and a naive eviction policy — say, pure recency-based LRU — will eventually slide past and evict the sink tokens, at which point the model has no valid drain and attention distributions become pathological even for tokens that are genuinely in the window.

What a beginner misses is the asymmetry: sink tokens are not important because of their content but because of their position in the attention geometry, and no eviction scoring function based on content relevance, recency, or frequency will naturally preserve them — you have to explicitly protect them as a special class. The expert worry is subtler still: in very long contexts, secondary sinks can form at chunk boundaries or after context injections, and an eviction policy that only protects the original BOS sink will gradually degrade because it doesn't know to preserve these emergent sinks, causing silent accuracy collapse rather than a clean failure.

The naive solution — maintain per-head eviction decisions — immediately collides with how KV caches are physically laid out: in virtually every production system (vLLM's paged attention, TensorRT-LLM's block manager), the unit of allocation is a block covering all heads at a given layer for a contiguous token range, so evicting a token for layer 8 while retaining it for layer 7 requires either duplicating the token's KV entries across separate per-head caches or accepting that you can only evict at the granularity of the coarsest retention requirement. ScissorHands and SnapKV move in a more surgical direction by computing per-head importance masks, but both still ultimately evict at the token level per layer, not per head per layer, meaning the retention decision is: keep this token's KV pair in layer L if the max (or weighted sum) importance across heads exceeds a threshold. The implication is that eviction decisions ideally belong at the (layer, head) granularity but are currently forced up to the (layer, token) granularity by memory allocator design — this is a systems-ML co-design gap, not just an algorithmic one. Closing it properly would require a disaggregated cache where each head maintains an independent paged pool, which multiplies allocator metadata overhead by the number of heads (typically 32–128) and makes cache-aware scheduling in a serving system like vLLM substantially harder; no production system does this today, which means every deployed eviction policy is implicitly making a suboptimal approximation when sink heterogeneity is high.

The deeper principled framing is to treat eviction as a secretary problem / optimal stopping problem: you observe tokens sequentially, each eviction is irrevocable, and you want to minimize the probability of discarding a token that future queries will need — the classical secretary solution (reject the first 1/e fraction, then keep the best seen so far) doesn't directly apply because importance is not i.i.d., but it motivates reservation policies that hold a protected buffer of recently-seen high-norm tokens as a hedge against context shifts. Fine-tuning absolutely destabilizes norm-based eviction signals, and the mechanism is concrete: when you fine-tune with a small domain-specific dataset, the key projection matrix W_K updates to amplify features that are discriminative for that domain, which inflates norms for tokens that are structurally common in fine-tuning data (e.g., specific delimiter patterns, domain jargon, formatting tokens) regardless of whether those tokens are semantically load-bearing during inference. Joint training is theoretically compelling and practically treacherous: the core difficulty is that eviction is a discrete selection operation — you either keep or drop a token — and discrete decisions are not differentiable, so naive backpropagation through an eviction step produces zero or undefined gradients exactly where you need signal. The standard workaround is straight-through estimators (STE) or Gumbel-softmax relaxation: during the forward pass you make a hard binary eviction decision, but during the backward pass you pretend the decision was a soft sigmoid or softmax and let gradients flow through — this is the approach used in learned token pruning work like LTP (Kim & Cho, 2021) and SpAtten, where importance predictors are trained with STE against a task loss, and it works well enough for pruning but introduces a train-inference mismatch because the model never actually sees the hard-evicted cache during training. A cleaner gradient pathway exists if you reframe eviction as differentiable subset selection via the PerturbedMax or SoftSort operators (Blondel et al., 2020), which give smooth approximations to top-k selection with well-defined gradients; this is more principled than STE but adds significant compute per training step and hasn't been applied to KV cache eviction at production scale as of mid-2025. The training objective is the real design challenge: optimizing directly against next-token perplexity couples eviction policy to the specific token distribution in training data, which risks overfitting the policy to training-domain attention patterns — a better objective might be eviction regret, defined as the KL divergence between attention distributions computed with full cache versus evicted cache, which is domain-agnostic and directly measures what eviction destroys. The systems implication is severe: joint training requires simulating cache pressure during training, which means artificially capping cache size, running sequences long enough to trigger eviction, and backpropagating through potentially hundreds of eviction decisions per sequence — this roughly doubles training memory and adds a hyperparameter (simulated cache size) that must match deployment conditions, which no current training framework (not Megatron-LM, not NeMo, not the standard HuggingFace training loop) supports natively.
